nodes.title: 1. Introduction
nodes.summary: LAFPP seeks a qualified CPA firm to audit its financial statements for fiscal years ending June 30, 2025–2027, with annual maximum fees and potential two one-year extensions. Proposers must have relevant large public pension-system experience; annual audits are required by state law and the City Charter, with State Controller guidelines informing compliance work. LAFPP administers defined-benefit pension and retiree health subsidy plans for Los Angeles police and firefighters, governed by a nine-member Board. It serves more than 27,000 members across six tiers, had approximately $33 billion in net assets as of December 2024, and includes a Section 115 OPEB trust. Simpson & Simpson audited fiscal years 2021–2024, and Segal prepared the 2024 actuarial valuation. Minimum qualifications include experienced key staff and a California-licensed engagement partner with governmental and large-plan expertise who directly supervises the work. Services cover financial-statement, investment, benefit, census, OPEB trust, and GASB 68/75 audits; opinions, findings, Board presentations, advisory support, deliverables, coordination, and working-paper retention.

nodes.title: 1.1 Purpose
nodes.summary: LAFPP seeks proposals from qualified certified public accounting firms to audit its financial statements for fiscal years ending June 30, 2025–2027. Proposers must have experience auditing large public pension or retirement systems with at least $5 billion in net assets. The intended contract is for three years, with a maximum fee proposed for each year; the Board may extend it through two one-year renewals. Firms should provide three-year pricing, and the award will follow the RFP’s terms and conditions. California Government Code Sections 7501–7504 require annual audited statements to be provided to the State Controller, and Los Angeles City Charter Section 362 also requires them. State Controller audit guidelines for public retirement systems are provided to help firms estimate the work needed to opine on compliance.

nodes.title: 1.2 Background
nodes.summary: LAFPP is one of three City of Los Angeles pension systems, administering pension and retiree health subsidy plans for sworn firefighters and police officers, including officers at Los Angeles World Airports and the Port of Los Angeles. It is governed under the City Charter and California Constitution by a nine-member Board: five mayoral appointees and four elected active or retired members, split equally between the departments. The Plan is a defined-benefit, single-employer plan operating under City Charter and Administrative Code provisions, with six tiers and over 27,000 active and retired members, including survivors. Its pensioner health subsidy plan is authorized by specified Charter and Administrative Code provisions. Net assets were approximately $33 billion at December 31, 2024 (unaudited), invested across public equities, fixed income, private equity and credit, real estate, and private infrastructure; fiscal 2024–25 pension and health expenses are projected at $1.66 billion. LAFPP established a Section 115 OPEB trust on July 1, 2022, included in its financial statements; as of June 2024, no separate opinion had been issued.

The Plan's Audited Financial Statements and Annual Actuarial Valuations are available at https://lafpp.lacity.gov/about/inside-lafpp/financial- reports.

key_items: 1.5.2 Perform annual audits of schedules related to GASB Statement No. 68,; 1.5.3 Provide related advisory services on:
1.5.2 Perform annual audits of schedules related to GASB Statement No. 68,
nodes.summary: The selected CPA firm will conduct annual audits of LAFPP’s Pension and Health Subsidy Plan financial statements under California public retirement system audit guidelines and Government Auditing Standards, issuing opinions and communicating error or fraud observations. Procedures include sampling member accounts and benefit payments; testing participant census data used for actuarial and GASB reporting; examining investment existence, valuation, and compliance with investment policies; auditing the IRC Section 115 OPEB trust; and performing subsequent-events work. The firm will report control deficiencies and efficiency or cost-saving opportunities, provide signed electronic statements and ten bound reports, present findings to the Board, and retain working papers for at least five years, making them available to LAFPP and successor auditors. It will also audit GASB 68 and 75 schedules, issue opinions, coordinate with LAFPP and City actuaries and external auditors, present results to the Board, and retain supporting records under the same terms. Advisory services cover GASB pension accounting and reporting, plus other needed advice.

nodes.title: 3. Detailed Submittal Requirements
nodes.summary: Proposals must follow the prescribed five-section format, be clear, complete, relevant, and properly labeled; submit required materials as a PDF by email, include a redacted copy when asserting public-records exemptions, and do not use City or LAFPP logos. The cover letter must provide proposer and authorized representative details, disclose exceptions and conflicts, include the non-collusion certification, and be signed by an appropriately authorized person. Include a table of contents. The questionnaire must reproduce and answer each question, with supporting page references, and address firm qualifications, experience, references, staffing, legal and conflict matters, security, policies, audit approach, transition, quality assurance, technical audit areas, risks, assistance, and disaster recovery/business continuity. Provide all-inclusive annual fees for required audit and advisory work over three years, plus hourly rates for as-needed services; estimates require prior LAFPP approval. Include all four specified appendix documents/forms; omissions may make the proposal nonresponsive.

nodes.title: 3.1 Proposal Format
key_items: 3.1.4 Proposers shall not use, copy, or replicate, in any form, the City of Los Angeles seal or LAFPP logo.
nodes.summary: Proposals must follow the specified format, be concise, accurate, complete, clear, and limited to relevant information, with all pages and visual materials numbered and labeled. Organize submissions into five sections: Cover Letter, Table of Contents, Proposal Questionnaire, Fee Structure, and Required Documents/Forms. Submit all applicable forms and supporting materials electronically as a PDF; missing required documentation may make a proposal nonresponsive. Email one copy labeled with the RFP title, number, and proposer’s company name. If claiming information is exempt from disclosure under the California Public Records Act, also provide a redacted copy. Proposers may not use or reproduce the City of Los Angeles seal or LAFPP logo.

nodes.title: 3.2 Proposal Section 1.0: Cover Letter
nodes.summary: The cover letter must identify the Proposer’s legal name, address, telephone number, and business status, and provide the authorized RFP/contract negotiation representative’s name, title, contact details, and any limits on authority. It must disclose exceptions to minimum requirements or RFP terms (which may affect evaluation or cause rejection) and any existing or potential conflicts of interest. It must include the required statement certifying the proposal is genuine and not sham or collusive, including that no one was induced to submit a sham bid or refrain from bidding and no collusive advantage was sought. The letter must be signed by someone authorized to bind the Proposer to the RFP, changes, and any resulting contract. Partnerships require a general partner’s signature; corporations require two specified authorized officers or an officer authorized by the board.

nodes.title: 3.3 Proposal Section 2.0: Table of Contents
nodes.summary:
3.3 Proposal Section 2.0: Table of Contents
Each proposal must include a Table of Contents listing the sections included in the proposal.

nodes.title: 3.4 Proposal Section 3.0: Proposal Questionnaire
nodes.summary: The questionnaire requires each question to be reproduced and answered, with page references for supporting attachments. Proposers must document relevant five-year government or pension-system experience, provide five qualifying references and contact details, and submit resumes and team roles, locations, experience, and qualifications; LAFPP may contact references and must approve staffing changes. Firm questions cover history, structure, licenses, staffing and turnover, rotation and retention, litigation, strengths, insurance, pension clients gained or lost, LAFPP relationships, data security and breaches, ownership certifications and outreach, non-audit services and conflict safeguards, requested contract changes, and harassment policies or litigation. Proposal responses must explain audit understanding, approach, transition, quality assurance, workload, complex investments, IRC Section 115 trusts, GASB and actuarial matters, required deadlines, and methods for auditing accounts, rolls, census data, IT, private-equity valuations, controls, and investment-policy compliance. They must also address startup, risks and remedies, requested LAFPP assistance, and other relevant information. Include a disaster recovery and business continuity plan covering risk assessment, impact analysis, strategy alignment, recovery objectives, testing, and updates.

nodes.title: 3.4.1 Demonstration of Minimum Qualifications
nodes.summary: The proposal questionnaire requires thorough answers immediately after each question and page references for any supporting attachments. To demonstrate minimum qualifications, proposers must describe relevant work over the past five years for government agencies or public pension systems and provide five references, each with plan net assets exceeding $5 billion, served by the proposed primary Engagement Partner or Audit Manager. For each reference, provide the client’s name and address, services, contract dates, primary partner or manager, and contact details. Submitting a proposal permits LAFPP to contact references. Provide the proposed Engagement Partner’s resume, covering title, relevant experience, licenses and certifications, current clients, public pension fund clients in the past five years, and California public pension clients in the past three years. Also identify audit-team members, office locations, and duties, and provide resumes with titles, functions, firm tenure in auditing, education, and public pension audit experience. LAFPP must approve subsequent changes to the engagement partner, supervisors, or other audit staff.

nodes.title: 3.4.2 About the Firm
nodes.summary: The section instructs firms to repeat and answer questions about: firm history, legal form, locations, services, staffing, ownership and anticipated changes; California public-accountancy licenses; management structure; five-year professional turnover; audit partner and manager rotation; employee recruitment and retention incentives; audit-related litigation or licensing actions; competitive strengths and suitability; fidelity, errors-and-omissions, and other insurance coverage, carriers, limits, and expiration dates; public employee retirement-system audit clients; clients lost in five years, service periods, and reasons; relationships with boards, staff, and council; past, current, or pending connections to LAFPP commissioners, consultants, or staff; data protection, breaches, and security of Social Security numbers and confidential information; government certifications as minority-, woman-, or other-owned enterprises and related outreach; non-audit services and conflict safeguards; requested changes to standard RFP or contract provisions; and sexual-harassment policies and related pending or anticipated misconduct litigation.

nodes.title: 3.4.3 Questions Concerning Your Proposal
nodes.summary: Proposals must show the firm’s understanding of the services and proposed approach, reproducing each question with its response. Questions cover the overall audit approach and transition from the prior auditor; understanding of scope and service levels; staff and audit quality assurance and the latest peer review; workload controls and concurrent-account limits; experience and resources for complex investments, IRC Section 115 trust funds, and GASB compliance, interpretation, accounting issues, and pension actuarial provisions. Firms must address meeting the required July interim fieldwork, October financial-statement submission, and second-week-of-November signed-report deadlines. They must explain approaches to auditing member accounts, retirement rolls, actuarial census data, IT systems, private-equity year-end valuations, internal controls, and investment-policy compliance. Responses should also describe startup work and timing, anticipated audit problems and remedies, requested LAFPP staff assistance, and any other pertinent information.

The DR/BCP shall include Risk Assessment, Business Impact Analysis, Alignment of Business Strategy, Alignment to

It lists annual fees for financial statement audit and advisory services (Section 1.5.1), GASB 68/75 audit (Section 1.5.2), and the total annual fee. key_items: 4.1.1 Level I: Review of Qualifications, Experience & References; 4.1.2 Level II: Administrative Responsiveness; 4.1.3 Level III: Proposed Services & Fees; 4.1.4 Level IV: Final Approval by the Board

nodes.summary: The proposal evaluation has four required stages: (1) review of qualifications, experience, references, minimum qualifications, contractor responsibility, and capacity to perform the services; (2) administrative responsiveness, including compliance with submission requirements and acceptance of LAFPP’s standard contract provisions; (3) evaluation and ranking of proposed services and fees; and (4) Board approval. The evaluation panel recommends the proposer offering the best overall value and strongest qualifications, but the Board of Fire and Police Pension Commissioners makes the final award decision at its sole discretion. Selection criteria include firm qualifications and experience, understanding of and ability to address LAFPP’s needs, cost reasonableness and value, and positive contracting history. LAFPP may also consider other appropriate criteria, whether or not stated in the RFP.

result.title: APPENDIX 6.2 STANDARD PROVISIONS  (Rev. 624 [v.1]).pdf
result.summary: The appendix sets standard provisions for City contracts, covering interpretation, California law and Los Angeles County venue, effectiveness, integration, written amendments, severability, and excusable delay, including mitigation and alternative sourcing. It governs waiver, suspension, convenience or cause termination, cure, immediate termination triggers, replacement-service costs, and post-termination duties; contractor independence, personnel, subcontracting, assignment, permits, labor and material claims, business-tax registration, records, audits, reports, and bonds. It addresses indemnity, intellectual-property ownership and licenses, data security and breach response, confidentiality, insurance, warranties, professional performance, and limits on payment to appropriated funds. Compliance requirements include nondiscrimination, equal benefits, affirmative action, child support, living wage, worker retention, union organizing, accessibility, contractor responsibility, slavery disclosure, hiring and local-business preferences, inclusion, Iran-related contracting, campaign contributions and lobbying, criminal-history restrictions, background checks for personnel supervising minors, payment-card and identity-theft protections, possessory-interest taxes, and workforce and ownership reporting. Applicable obligations must flow down to subcontractors; violations may trigger remedies or termination.

nodes.summary: Attachment A (June 2024 revision) contains standard provisions for City contracts, PSC-1 through PSC-44, plus insurance requirements. Topics include contract interpretation, applicable law and venue, effectiveness, integration and amendments, excusable delays, waiver, suspension and termination; contractor independence, personnel, assignment, permits, labor/material claims, business-tax registration, records/audits, bonds, indemnity, intellectual property, ownership, data protection, insurance, warranties, and payment limits. It also addresses non-discrimination, child support, living-wage and worker-retention rules, accessibility, contractor responsibility, inclusion, slavery disclosure, hiring and local-business preferences, Iran-related contracting, campaign contributions, criminal-history use, identity-theft and payment-card security, public-resource requirements, possessory-interest tax, confidentiality, and contractor data reporting. The excerpt explains that headings do not control meaning; terms are fairly construed, plural and joint-and-several obligations may apply, and genders are inclusive. California law governs, applicable laws must be followed without extra compensation for changes, and actions belong in Los Angeles County courts; invalid provisions do not void the remainder. The contract takes effect after required signatures and approvals, supersedes prior understandings, and amendments must be written and approved. Force majeure may excuse faultless, uncontrollable delays.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary:
CONTRACTOR shall not constitute a Force Majeure Event, unless the delay or failure arises out of causes beyond the control of both CONTRACTOR and Subcontractor, and without any fault or negligence of either of them. In such case, CONTRACTOR shall not be liable for the delay or failure to perform, unless the goods or services to be furnished by the Subcontractor were obtainable from other sources in sufficient time to permit CONTRACTOR to perform timely. As used in this Contract, the term "Subcontractor" means a subcontractor at any tier.
In the event CONTRACTOR’S delay or failure to perform arises out of a Force Majeure Event, CONTRACTOR agrees to use commercially reasonable best efforts to obtain the goods or services from other sources, and to otherwise mitigate the damages and reduce the delay caused by the Force Majeure Event.

nodes.title: PSC-7. Waiver
key_items: B. Termination for Breach of Contract
nodes.summary: A waiver does not waive later defaults or the underlying contract term, and continued performance after default is not a waiver. The City may suspend services by written notice; the contractor must stop and incur no further costs until resumption is authorized. The City may terminate for convenience on 30 days’ notice, paying allowable costs through termination and necessary termination costs; contract materials and entitled intellectual property become City property. Breach termination requires notice and any City-directed cure opportunity, with separate immediate suspension for uninsured services. Immediate termination may follow insolvency proceedings, creditor assignments, dishonest conduct, or lobbying violations. Moral-turpitude rules require prompt notice of charges or related outcomes and permit termination under specified conditions; covered crimes and Key Persons are defined. The City may obtain replacement services and recover costs and damages; excusable or nonexistent default converts termination to convenience, without limiting remedies. The contractor must notify employees, subcontractors, and other contracted parties upon termination. It is an independent contractor; City controls personnel and subcontractor approval, while contractor remains responsible for performance and payment. Assignment or delegation requires prior written City consent.

nodes.title: PSC-13. Permits
nodes.summary: The contractor and its personnel and subcontractors must obtain and maintain all documents required to perform the contract and immediately notify the City of any related suspension, termination, lapse, nonrenewal, or restriction. The contractor must pay labor and material costs and applicable unemployment and other legal obligations when due to prevent claims or liens against City property. It must maintain valid Los Angeles business tax registration certificates throughout the contract. Contract and financial records must be kept in their original or City-approved form for at least three years after the latest of final payment, expiration, or termination, and be available for City examination and audit at any time. The contractor must provide requested performance reports, include the same recordkeeping provision in subcontracts, or, with the City’s written approval, submit the required information electronically at contract expiration or termination instead of retaining the records.

nodes.title: PSC-17. Bonds
nodes.summary: Required bonds must be filed with the City Administrative Officer’s Risk Management for review and acceptance under applicable LAAC provisions. Contractor must defend and indemnify the City against claims and costs arising from contractor or subcontractor acts or omissions, except for the City’s active negligence or willful misconduct; remedies are cumulative and the obligation survives termination. Contractor must also indemnify the City for actual or alleged intellectual-property infringement involving materials used or work products supplied, warrant non-infringement, and provide surviving, cumulative remedies. Contract work products belong exclusively to the City, with worldwide intellectual-property rights assigned; contractor must assist in documenting ownership, may not disclose work products without written consent, and must flow these protections to subcontractors. The City may seek injunctions or specific performance. For externally created work products, contractor must obtain a free, perpetual, nonexclusive City-use license. Contractor must secure City data using commercially available strongest protections, report breaches or security incidents within 24 hours, remediate immediately, provide updates, investigate and share findings, and cooperate with City and law enforcement; the City may lead or join investigations.

nodes.title: B. If CITY is subject to liability for any Data Breach or Security Incident, then
nodes.summary: If the City is liable for a data breach or security incident, the contractor must indemnify, defend, and hold it harmless. The contractor must maintain required insurance and bonds, offer the City its best available terms, and perform professionally. Requirements include nondiscrimination, equal benefits and employment, affirmative action, child-support orders and reporting, living-wage, worker-retention, union-organizing, contractor-responsibility, slavery-disclosure, first-source hiring, local-business preference, criminal-history, and accessibility laws; applicable terms must flow down to subcontractors. Defaults may lead to termination after notice and an opportunity to cure. Business Inclusion Program outreach, subcontractor-change approval, Iran-contracting affidavits, and campaign-contribution, fundraising, disclosure, and subcontractor-notice rules also apply. City payment is limited to appropriated funds. Contractors must protect payment data under identity-theft, FACTA, and PCI rules; obtain required background checks for personnel supervising minors; pay applicable possessory-interest taxes; protect confidential information and report access attempts; and provide contractor and subcontractor workforce and ownership data. Insurance provisions address coverage, notice, approval, and consequences for lapses; bidder certifications address covered contracts and lobbying disclosures.

nodes.title: B. If CITY is subject to liability for any Data Breach or Security Incident, then (intro)
nodes.summary: If the City is liable for a data breach or security incident, the contractor must indemnify, defend, and hold the City harmless. The contractor must maintain, at its expense, insurance meeting City Risk Management’s coverage, limits, and contractual requirements, incorporated by reference. Throughout the contract, it must offer the City its best terms, prices, and discounts available to other customers for similar goods and services, and perform work to professional standards. Unless exempt, it must comply with applicable nondiscrimination, equal benefits, equal employment practices, and affirmative action laws; discrimination in hiring or employment is prohibited on listed protected grounds. Relevant LAAC provisions are incorporated, and identical terms must appear in subcontracts. The contractor must also comply with the Child Support Assignment Orders Ordinance and employment-reporting requirements, and implement legally served wage or earnings assignments. Noncompliance by the contractor or a principal owner constitutes contract default; the text ends while describing failure to cure.

nodes.title: Contractor Warranty and Compliance Requirements
nodes.summary: The contractor warrants that its work will meet professional standards for comparable work and circumstances. Unless exempt, the contract is subject to applicable Los Angeles non-discrimination, equal benefits, equal employment practices, and affirmative action requirements. The contractor must comply with applicable federal, California, and City laws and may not discriminate in hiring or employment on the listed protected grounds. Relevant LAAC provisions are incorporated, and identical requirements must appear in subcontracts. The contractor must also comply with the Child Support Assignment Orders Ordinance and employment-reporting requirements. Noncompliance with reporting or assignment orders, including orders applicable to principal owners, constitutes contract default; the text ends while describing failure to cure.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: The contractor warrants that work will meet professional standards for comparable work and circumstances. It must comply with applicable federal, California, and City nondiscrimination and affirmative-action laws, prohibit employment discrimination on listed protected grounds, and follow incorporated LAAC Equal Benefits, Equal Employment Practices, and Affirmative Action Program requirements; subcontractors must accept identical provisions. It must meet child-support assignment and employment-reporting requirements; noncompliance, including by a principal owner, is default, and failure to cure within 90 days of notice may lead to termination. It must comply with the Living Wage and Service Contractor Worker Retention ordinances and federal protections against retaliation for union organizing, with identical subcontract clauses. Accessibility obligations include compliance with disability, rehabilitation, fair-housing, and related laws; no disability-based discrimination, including association-based discrimination; reasonable accommodation for equal access to City-funded services; UFAS-compliant construction; and accessible facilities under applicable ADA and California standards. The City relies on these certifications, which subcontractors must also adopt.

nodes.title: Contractor Labor and Accessibility Obligations
nodes.summary: Failure to remedy a default within 90 days after notice may result in contract termination for breach. Subcontracts must include the same applicable provisions. The contractor must comply with the Living Wage Ordinance and federal protections against retaliation for union organizing, as well as the Service Contractor Worker Retention Ordinance. It must also comply with disability-access laws, refrain from disability-related discrimination, provide reasonable accommodations for equal access to City-funded services, and ensure construction and service facilities meet applicable federal and state accessibility standards. The City relies on these accessibility certifications and representations as a condition of funding.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: The text states that failure to cure a default within 90 days after notice may terminate the contract for breach, and requires the provision in subcontracts. Contractors must comply with the Living Wage, Service Contractor Worker Retention, Contractor Responsibility, Slavery Disclosure, First Source Hiring, and Local Business Preference ordinances; specified provisions must also appear in subcontracts. Living Wage compliance includes federal protections against retaliation for union organizing. Contractors must meet disability-accessibility laws, avoid disability discrimination, provide reasonable accommodations, ensure accessible construction and facilities, and pass these requirements to subcontractors; the City relies on these certifications. Unless exempted, contractors must follow the Business Inclusion Program, document outreach to diverse businesses through BAVN, and obtain City approval before changing designated subcontractors or their work or effort. Contracts of at least $1 million require an Iran Contracting Act compliance affidavit. For contracts of at least $100,000 requiring elected-office approval, campaign-contribution and fundraising restrictions apply to the contractor, relevant principals, and qualifying subcontractors and their principals.

nodes.title: City Contractor Ordinance and Compliance Requirements
nodes.summary: Contractors must comply with the Contractor Responsibility Ordinance. The Business Inclusion Program requires compliance unless exempted before bid submission, documented outreach to Minority, Women, and Other Business Enterprises through BAVN, and City approval before changing designated subcontractors, their pledged work, or effort levels. Subcontracts must include identical provisions requiring compliance with the Slavery Disclosure, First Source Hiring, and Local Business Preference Ordinances. Contracts for goods or services estimated at $1 million or more require an Iran Contracting Act compliance affidavit. The page also begins campaign contribution and fundraising restrictions for nonexempt contracts worth at least $100,000 requiring approval by an elected City office, identifying the contractor, its principals, qualifying subcontractors, and their principals as restricted persons; the provision continues beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: Contractor must comply with the Contractor Responsibility, Slavery Disclosure, First Source Hiring, Local Business Preference, and criminal-history employment ordinances; the latter four must be included identically in subcontracts. Unless exempt, it must meet the Business Inclusion Program throughout the contract, use BAVN to conduct and document outreach to diverse businesses, and obtain City approval before changing designated subcontractors, work, or effort. Contracts of at least $1 million require an Iran Contracting Act compliance affidavit. For qualifying contracts of at least $100,000 requiring elected-office approval, contractors, relevant principals, and major subcontractors face 12-month campaign-contribution and fundraising restrictions, disclosure requirements, and mandatory subcontractor notice and principal-information provisions; violations may lead to termination and legal remedies. City payment is contingent on prior appropriation: services, purchases, or expenses beyond appropriated funds are unpaid, and the contractor is not required to provide services beyond that funding.

nodes.title: Campaign Restrictions and Contractual Obligations
nodes.summary: The text requires compliance with City campaign-contribution and fundraising restrictions, which apply to certain restricted persons for 12 months after contract signing; violations may lead to termination and legal remedies. Covered contractors must submit and update Ethics Commission Form 55 and include a specified notice in contracts with subcontractors expected to receive at least $100,000, requiring disclosure and timely updates of principals’ contact information. Contractors must also comply with the City ordinance governing use of criminal history in employment applications and include the same requirement in subcontracts. The City is not required to pay unless it has appropriated sufficient funds; services, purchases, or expenses exceeding appropriations are provided without charge, and the contractor has no obligation to provide services beyond them.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: Contractors and restricted persons must comply with City campaign-contribution and fundraising restrictions lasting 12 months after contract signing; violations may lead to termination and legal remedies. Covered contractors must file and update Ethics Commission Form 55, and include the specified notice in subcontracts of at least $100,000, requiring subcontractors to disclose and update principals’ contact information. PSC-38 requires compliance with the City criminal-history employment ordinance and identical subcontract terms. PSC-39 limits City payment to appropriated funds; excess services, purchases, and expenses are unpaid, and contractors need not perform beyond appropriations until additional funds are approved. PSC-40 requires compliance with identity-theft laws, FACTA, and PCI DSS, including verifying receipt truncation when servicing payment devices. PSC-41, where applicable, requires DOJ fingerprint and background checks at the contractor’s expense for personnel supervising or disciplining minors at specified recreational facilities. PSC-42 warns that City-granted rights may create taxable possessory interests, which the contractor must pay if applicable; statutory notice is acknowledged.

nodes.title: Contractor Compliance, Background Checks, and Taxes
nodes.summary: Contractor may not provide equipment or incur expenses beyond appropriated amounts until the City appropriates additional funds. Under PSC-40, Contractor must comply with identity-theft laws, including payment-device, card-fraud, and FACTA receipt requirements, and maintain PCI DSS compliance; when installing, programming, or updating payment devices, it must verify proper receipt truncation. Under PSC-41, when applicable, Contractor must follow California Public Resources Code Section 5164 and City rules. Personnel—including subcontractor personnel—with supervisory or disciplinary authority over minors at covered recreational premises must pass a California Department of Justice fingerprint and background check, at Contractor’s expense, confirming no specified disqualifying convictions. Under PSC-42, City-granted rights may create a taxable possessory interest; Contractor must pay any applicable property tax and acknowledges receipt of the legally required notice.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: Contractor may not provide equipment or incur expenses beyond appropriated amounts until the City appropriates additional funds. It must comply with identity-theft laws, FACTA receipt requirements, and PCI DSS, and verify proper receipt truncation when installing, programming, or updating payment devices. Where applicable, it must follow California Public Resources Code § 5164 and City rules, ensuring personnel and subcontractor personnel with authority over minors at covered sites pass DOJ fingerprint and background checks at Contractor’s expense. City-granted rights may create a taxable possessory interest, which Contractor must pay tax on if applicable; required tax notice is acknowledged. Documents and information supplied by the City or developed under the contract are confidential and may be disclosed only with City authorization or as required by law.

nodes.title: CONTRACTOR
nodes.summary: Contractor must promptly notify the City of third-party attempts to access confidential information; this duty survives contract expiration or termination. For-profit privately owned contractors must report their and subcontractors’ annual revenue, employee count, location, industry, and majority owner’s race/ethnicity and gender within 30 days after the contract starts and annually thereafter through RAMP or another City-approved method, and request annual subcontractor profile updates. Insurance provisions provide City risk-management contacts and bond/insurance assistance options. They require City additional-insured/loss-payee status as applicable; cancellation/reduction notice; primary, noncontributing coverage; possible coverage changes with 90 days’ notice and negotiation of substantial added costs; advance approval; workers’ compensation compliance; eligible California insurers; reporting and restoring impaired aggregates; and coverage effective when performance steps begin. Failure to maintain insurance may result in suspension, termination, or City-purchased coverage charged to Contractor. A schedule lists required limits and potential coverage types, including workers’ compensation, liability, auto, professional, property, pollution, bonds, and crime. The bidder certification form covers qualifying contract types, lobbying disclosure compliance, and certification under penalty of perjury.

result.title: Form 50 - Bidder Certification (rev. 02_2022).pdf
result.summary: The text contains two Los Angeles City bid forms. The Bidder Certification form must accompany a bid or proposal and collects filing status, awarding department, reference number, bidder contact details, and signed certification. It covers goods/services contracts over $25,000 lasting at least three months; construction contracts of any value or duration; qualifying financial-assistance contracts of at least $100,000; and public leases or licenses of any value. The bidder agrees to applicable lobbying-ordinance disclosure rules and certifies the information under penalty of perjury. The Prohibited Contributors form must be completed and submitted with the bid; it collects solicitation and bidder details, asks whether Schedule A principals and Schedule B subcontractors with subcontracts worth $100,000 or more apply, and records total pages submitted. The signer certifies compliance with and notification of Charter § 470(c)(12) restrictions, promises to amend the form within ten business days of changes, and attests to authority and accuracy under penalty of perjury. Both forms include signature fields, Ethics Commission contact information, and February 2022 revision references.

result.title: Form 55 - Prohibited Contributors (Bidders) (rev. 02_2022).pdf
result.summary: Form 55 (Bidders), revised February 2022, is a required Prohibited Contributors disclosure submitted in full with a bid or proposal; omissions may affect the submission. It records bid and contract details, awarding authority, bidder contact information, principal and qualifying-subcontractor disclosures, and page count. The bidder certifies under penalty of perjury that it understands and will comply with applicable City requirements, has notified principals and subcontractors, will update changed information within 10 business days, and provides truthful, complete information. Schedule A lists bidder principals—the specified senior executives, owners with at least 20% interest, and employees authorized to represent the bidder before the City. Schedule B separately identifies subcontractors with contracts of $100,000 or more and, where applicable, their principals. The section also presents LAFPP’s Contractor Disclosure Policy: it promotes transparency and merit-based decisions through timely, complete disclosure of relevant communications, relationships, and payments, including potentially influential ex parte communications. It applies to contractor application, selection, and monitoring, supplements applicable laws, and addresses selection participants and agreements entered after July 23, 2009.

nodes.title: Schedule Summary
nodes.summary: Form 55(Bidders) is a required Prohibited Contributors form to submit in full with a bid or proposal to the awarding City department; an incomplete or missing form may affect the submission. It provides Ethics Commission contact information and fields for original and amendment dates, bid/contract reference and submission date, contract description, awarding authority, and bidder name, address, email, and phone. The schedule summary requires responses on whether the bidder has principals (as defined by LAMC § 49.7.35(A)(6); entities must have at least one, and a “Yes” requires Schedule A) and subcontractors with subcontracts worth $100,000 or more (a “Yes” requires Schedule B), plus the total pages submitted.

nodes.title: Certification
nodes.summary: The certification, made under penalty of perjury under Los Angeles City and California law, confirms the signer understands and will comply with Los Angeles City Charter § 470(c)(12) and related ordinances, has notified principals and subcontractors of the requirements, will amend the form within 10 business days if information changes, is the named bidder or authorized representative, and believes the information is true and complete. It provides spaces for name, signature, title, and date, and cites the applicable laws. The form is titled “Prohibited Contributors 55 (Bidders),” was revised February 2022, and is page 1 of 3.

nodes.title: Schedule A - Bidder’s Principals
nodes.summary: Schedule A asks bidders to list each principal’s name, title, and address. Principals include the board chair, president, CEO, COO or functional equivalents; anyone with at least 20% ownership; and employees authorized to represent the bidder before the City. The form provides multiple entry lines and a checkbox to indicate attached additional pages. It is revised February 2022 and cites Los Angeles City Charter § 470(c)(12) and Los Angeles Municipal Code §§ 49.7.35(B)(3)–(4); it is page 2 of 3 of the Prohibited Contributors form for bidders.

nodes.title: Schedule B - Subcontractors and Their Principals
nodes.summary: Schedule B requires disclosure of each subcontractor with a subcontract worth $100,000 or more, using a separate page per subcontractor. It collects the subcontractor’s name and address and whether it has principals; if yes, list each principal’s name, title, and address. Principals include specified senior executives or equivalents, owners holding at least 20%, and employees authorized to represent the subcontractor before the City. Additional pages may be attached. The form cites Los Angeles ethics laws and is revised February 2022. The text also presents LAFPP’s Contractor Disclosure Policy, whose purpose is to disclose actual, potential, and perceived conflicts, promote transparency, and keep decisions based on merit. It requires timely, full disclosure of certain communications, relationships, and payments involving intermediaries; applies broadly and supplements applicable state and City laws. Ex parte communications that could appear influential are disclosable even if they do not constitute undue influence. The policy covers contractor application, selection, and monitoring, including selection participants and agreements entered after July 23, 2009; the passage ends while addressing existing agreements.

result.title: APPENDIX 6.5 LAFPP CONTRACTOR DISCLOSURE POLICY.pdf
result.summary: The section sets out LAFPP’s Contractor Disclosure Policy: its purpose, legal context, scope, exclusions, reporting schedules, and disclosure requirements for campaign contributions, other payments, gifts, official contacts, and intermediaries. It identifies covered contractors, personnel, family members, recipients, and required disclosure details, including special reporting rules for investment managers and consultants. It assigns duties to contractors, LAFPP section managers, and Internal Audit for accurate, timely filings, due diligence, Board reporting, and intermediary fees. Material violations may lead to reimbursement, termination, or exclusion from future contracting; disclosures are public records. The section also provides policy definitions and gift exclusions, adoption and revision history, and review timing. Appendix A further explains insurance-document submission, required coverage and endorsements, cancellation notices, electronic filing and verification, renewals, and separate review of alternative-risk or self-insurance programs.

nodes.title: A. PURPOSE
nodes.summary: LAFPP’s Contractor Disclosure Policy requires contractors to disclose actual, potential, and perceived conflicts of interest to prevent impropriety, promote transparency and confidence, and ensure investment and procurement decisions are based on merit. It requires full, timely disclosure of specified ex parte communications, relationships, and payments involving intermediaries such as placement agents, marketers, and lobbyists, and broadly covers current or prospective contractors. The policy supplements applicable City and California ethics, campaign-finance, and lobbying laws; undefined terms generally follow Appendix A. While communication through staff between contractors or consultants and Board members is recognized as beneficial, direct communications that could appear to influence decisions or recommendations must be disclosed because they may cause misunderstanding, misinformation, or conflicting instructions—even if they do not constitute undue influence.

nodes.title: B. APPLICATION, EXCLUSIONS AND REPORTING
nodes.summary: The policy governs LAFPP’s contractor selection and monitoring, covering all contractors participating in contract selection, agreements entered after July 23, 2009, and existing agreements when extended, additional funds are committed, or substantive terms are amended with LAFPP’s consent. Exclusions include authorized contracts of $25,000 or less for up to one year; equipment maintenance or repair costing $2,000 or less; contracts under three months; use of existing City, state, or federal agreements; and union or association contracts for LAFPP-subsidized health plans. For new contracts and investments, contractors disclose reportable items from the preceding 24 months; relevant fund managers do so when new or additional investments are considered. Existing contractors generally file quarterly disclosures within 21 business days after each quarter; the latest disclosure is required for renewals/extensions, and internal audit reviews disclosures for Board reporting. Real Estate Open-End Fund managers also file quarterly. Private equity, private credit, and Real Estate Closed-End Fund managers file annual gift disclosures within 21 business days after year-end, not contractor disclosures except for new or increased investments. Non-investment, non-legal contractors paid $20,000 or less annually disclose within 21 business days after June 30; internal audit determines reporting frequency and notifies firms of changes.

nodes.title: C. CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS
nodes.summary: Contractors must disclose monetary contributions and other financial benefits made directly or indirectly to Elected Officials and their controlled committees, Candidates and their controlled committees, Appointed Officials, or Applicable City Employees. The requirement covers the Contractor, specified personnel involved with services or products provided or sought for LAFPP, Intermediaries, and their Family Members. Each disclosure must identify the contributor and address and connection to the Contractor; each recipient’s name and title and the official, candidate, or person benefiting; the amount; and the date. Contributions or benefits are exempt if made by someone entitled to vote for the relevant Elected Official or Candidate at the time, and total no more than $100 to that person per election.

nodes.title: D. OTHER CONTRIBUTIONS/PAYMENTS
nodes.summary: Contractors must disclose all monetary contributions and other financial benefits not covered elsewhere in the Policy, including charitable contributions. Disclosures cover benefits to elected officials, candidates, their controlled committees, appointed officials, applicable City employees, City Council-created accounts or trusts seeking funds controlled by officials or candidates, third parties acting at their behest or supporting/opposing officials, candidates, or City ballot measures, and payments to officials or employees for private-property sales. They also cover contributions to organizations or individuals at an official’s or employee’s behest, including organizations where that person is known to hold a leadership, employment, or board role. Requirements apply to the Contractor and relevant officers, marketing or relationship representatives, portfolio managers, investment committee members, intermediaries involved in LAFPP-related products or services, and their family members. Each disclosure must state the contributor’s name, address, and connection to the Contractor; each recipient’s name and title and the beneficiary’s name; the amount or value; and the date.

nodes.title: E. GIFTS
nodes.summary: Contractors must disclose gifts made directly or indirectly to elected or appointed officials, candidates, applicable City employees, and decision makers at LAFPP’s specified investment consultants. The rules cover contractors and involved officers, representatives, portfolio managers, investment committee members, intermediaries, and their family members. Gifts worth at least $50 to one person, individually or cumulatively from one source in a calendar year, are reportable; contractors must track gifts. Reporting is annual for private equity, private credit, and real estate closed-end fund managers; quarterly for other existing contractors; and, for initial contractor disclosures, before Board approval, covering the prior 24 months. Each report identifies the giver and connection to the contractor, recipient and title, value, description, and date. LAFPP consultants must also report qualifying gifts received by decision makers from covered contractor-related persons, tracking cumulative gifts. They report gifts received during their LAFPP service agreement quarterly for all contractors, or as LAFPP requires for a particular contracting process, with the same details.

nodes.title: F. CONTACT STATEMENT
nodes.summary: Contractors must disclose to staff, before hiring for new agreements or investments, contacts with appointed or elected officials made during the longer of the three months before the interview or the search period, including dates, names, and nature of contacts; intermediary disclosures are covered separately. For existing agreements, contractors must report such contacts quarterly during the agreement, contract, or investment term, except entities excluded under Section 1.18.B.3b. The excerpt is under “Ethics Responsibilities for Board Members, the General Manager, and Staff.”

nodes.title: G. INTERMEDIARIES
nodes.summary: Contractors must include intermediary disclosures in initial and periodic Contractor Disclosures. They must identify whether anyone working on or assigned to an LAFPP contract, or that person’s family member, is a current or former LAFPP Board member, employee, or consultant. They must state whether specified Contractor personnel or their family members have compensated or agreed to compensate anyone acting as an intermediary for LAFPP investments or procurements, and describe compensation to intermediaries or employees hired to solicit or paid for LAFPP business, including its nature, timing, amount, and conditions. For each intermediary, disclose its services and client-use scope; principals’ qualifications and investment experience; written and oral agreements; contacts with LAFPP officials or staff during the 24 months before Board approval; who recommended it and how it was selected; and its and affiliates’ securities-industry and government lobbyist registrations, with details or an explanation if registration is not required.

nodes.title: H. CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES
nodes.summary: Contractors must provide a signed CEO, qualifying officer, or relevant business-unit head’s warranty that Contractor Disclosure information in the final agreement is accurate; comply and cooperate with the Policy, interpreting uncertainty in favor of disclosure; and submit disclosures to LAFPP Internal Audit by email or the listed Los Angeles office within 21 business days after the applicable quarter or year. LAFPP section managers must provide the Policy with RFPs when due diligence begins, verify receipt before due diligence concludes or an engagement, investment, or procurement is recommended or decided, and ensure agreements make Contractors solely responsible for Intermediary fees and expenses. They must exclude Contractors or Intermediaries following Board-determined material violations for up to five years and promptly notify the Board. Internal Audit must provide disclosures to the Board before decisions, prepare quarterly reports on Intermediary compensation, contributions and gifts, contacts, exclusions, and outstanding disclosures, and immediately report reasonably suspected material violations.

nodes.title: J. PENALTIES
nodes.summary: For new or amended agreements, contractors must accept remedies for material disclosure omissions/inaccuracies or other policy violations, as determined by the Board: reimbursement of the greater of one year’s fees or payments promised to an intermediary; penalty-free termination of investment or other agreements; and possible bans from future contracting. Contractors and materially violating intermediaries are ineligible for and may not solicit LAFPP contracts for five years, subject to reduction by a Board majority vote in public session for good cause. Contractor disclosures and attachments are public records under California’s Public Records Act and Ralph M. Brown Act, with no confidentiality restrictions. The text references Appendix A for definitions, lists policy adoption and revision dates from 2009 through 2024, and requires review every February of even-numbered years, except Marketing Cessation, reviewed annually.

nodes.title: Disclosure Confidentiality and Policy History
nodes.summary: A penalty may be reduced by a majority Board vote in public session upon good cause. Contractor disclosures and attachments are public records under the California Public Records Act and Ralph M. Brown Act, with no confidentiality restrictions; see Appendix A for definitions. The policy was adopted July 23, 2009, and revised on February 4, 2010; March 3, 2011; April 5, 2012; June 4, 2015; November 3, 2016; October 5, 2017; May 20 and August 5, 2021; November 2, 2023; and February 1, 2024.

result.title: APPENDIX 6.6 SUBMITTING PROOF OF INSURANCE.pdf

Electronic submission through KwikComply using ACORD 25 is required, with authorized evidence, cancellation notice, and applicable additional-insured endorsements; renewals and verification also use the system.
